extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of media studies/journalism; instructors and researchers examining external influences on news/media content
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and describe how external forces (advertisers, target audiences, governments, sponsors, technology) shape media content and organizational choices in commercial and state systems. Useful for teaching, analysis, and policy discussion about news/homepage content influences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising rates and circulation ('cost per thousand')
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertising rates are computed according to how many audience members use the medium—what is often called 'cost per thousand'—so having more subscribers means more advertising income for the magazine or newspaper, up to a point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Circulation audit rules limit free issues after subscription expiration to assure advertisers that claimed circulation is valued. There is a limit where additional advertising revenue from new subscribers cannot cover distribution costs (example: some mass-circulation weeklies such as Life shifted to monthly as costs and TV competition rose).

rubrics_metrics.name: Target audience / market definition
rubrics_metrics.description: That segment of the mass audience most likely to buy advertisers' products is called the target audience or market; target audiences are defined in terms of demographics (age, gender, income, education) or psychographics (attitudes and lifestyles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advertisers buy space/time from media with the best target audience for their products. Media 'find out what target audience members want and then give it to them' (Flow). Examples: newspapers shifting toward upscale 'champagne crowd' readers (Wall Street Journal, Boston Globe statistics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Media capture of the 'right' target audience
rubrics_metrics.description: A medium's content and marketing choices are judged by whether they capture the 'right' target audience for advertisers—media that best match advertisers' desired demographics/psychographics are preferred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers may structure news content and concentrate circulation drives in neighborhoods predicted to yield favorable demographics. Example: intentional content structuring and selective marketing to cultivate high-income readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalists' knowledge of and orientation toward audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: The process of socialization in an advertiser-funded medium should draw journalists' attention toward the audiences they write for, but journalists often have little or incorrect knowledge about their audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Circulation and advertising sales departments provide a 'picture of the audience,' yet studies show journalists often do not know their audiences; journalists may attribute more influence to their own opinions than to editors or readers. Minority journalists may lack 'cultural literacy' about their ethnic communities, affecting coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Targeting ethnic (Hispanic/Latino) audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisers increasingly target Hispanic audiences due to growing disposable income; mainstream media producing content attractive to Hispanics affects Hispanic-targeted publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advertisers care whether 'the client's image [will] be enhanced by advertising' in a Latino publication—mere ethnic publication is not enough. Competition from mainstream outlets (joint ventures, insertion into mainstream papers) can threaten ethnic publications' survival; advice to ethnic publishers includes improving content and market research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Targeting female audiences / making content relevant to women
rubrics_metrics.description: Women readers want topics and presentation relevant to their daily lives (children's education, time/money saving, safety/health, women in workplace, social concerns, family/relationships) and they want information that is useful, easy to find, and deep.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newspapers aiming to attract women redesign beats to be less dependent on officials and more on everyday impacts; they reframe government and education stories to emphasize effects on people's lives. Avoid emphasizing 'superwomen' profiles that may alienate many women; be sensitive when reporting on disasters/crime to avoid invading privacy or insensitivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailoring editions via technology to deliver ads
rubrics_metrics.description: New technologies can 'tailor' an edition (e.g., subscribers ordering only sections) so that ads go only to readers likely to buy the advertised product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Software could handle sorting of subscribers' section orders, but the mechanical and labeling requirements are more difficult. Tailoring aims for more efficient ad delivery to targeted readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertisers' financial influence ('advertisers' muscle')
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisers use their financial muscle to protest perceived unfair treatment by the news media; threats to pull ads and actual ad withdrawals are common and can influence editorial choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surveys show editors report advertiser threats and ad withdrawals in response to unfavorable coverage; this pressure can shift media toward reliance on press releases and self-censorship. Examples: tobacco industry ad withdrawals, Saatchi & Saatchi dropping accounts to placate big clients, GM pulling advertising over Dateline NBC segment (led to apology and settlement). Networks consider aggregate advertiser tolerance when scheduling/approving programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertiser-created programming and relinquished creative control
rubrics_metrics.description: Program-length commercials and advertiser-created shows are conceived primarily as vehicles to provide product exposure; creative control is typically relinquished to the product manufacturer, who dictates character portrayal, dialogue, and settings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This trend intensified in deregulated climates (1980s). Examples include children's programming conceived to sell toys, videocassettes and cable channels filled with advertiser-produced content, Macy's proposed cable channel devoted to selling store merchandise. Such programming intertwines commercials and information to prevent skipping or erasing advertising messages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Growth of infomercials and direct-response long-form advertising
rubrics_metrics.description: Since the late 1980s there has been growth in 30-minute advertising productions ('infomercials') that sell products directly via endorsements, celebrity testimonials, and toll-free ordering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Infomercials accounted for substantial ad revenue (example: over $750 million in 1994). They blur the line between advertising and program content and can be very effective sales channels (examples: Victoria Jackson sales).

rubrics_metrics.name: Blurring of advertising and editorial content
rubrics_metrics.description: Ads or paid material can cross the line into editorial content; news organizations may cover or lead with advertising-related material, and political actors may produce 'newsworthy' content to gain free exposure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News media's interest in political advertising can lead to campaign-produced material being treated as news (quote from Roger Ailes). Editorial decisions can be influenced by the attractiveness of advertisers or the potential for content to package commercials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government controls over media (laws, regulations, licenses, taxes, financing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Governments exert controls over mass media through laws, regulations, licensing, taxes in privately-owned systems, and through financing in government-owned systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control ranges from heavy censorship and repression to more limited regulatory oversight. Freedom House and other studies document press-freedom violations worldwide; country comparisons show varying inclinations to control the press (examples: states with high control vs low control).

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods of censorship, repression, and harassment
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods include forbidding journalists to write or sign articles, travel and passport restrictions, arrests, kidnappings, physical assaults, death threats and killings, banning publications, revoking press credentials, and ordering broadcasters not to carry certain statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Algerian reprisals against journalists, South African censorship efforts, Australian High Court ordering source disclosure, UK bans on broadcasting statements by specified groups, Israel's shutdowns and credential revocations, and killings during conflicts (Russia 1993). Statistical summaries illustrate scale of press-freedom violations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technology's effect on censorship and state control
rubrics_metrics.description: Technologies such as satellite TV, cable, videotape, and the growth of video rental outlets can undermine government censorship by providing alternative sources of information and making control more difficult.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Governments may attempt to block technologies (example: India considering preventing private cable companies from using satellite dishes to capture foreign signals like CNN), but technology can also increase foreign coverage of censored events (South Africa example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory restrictions on journalist qualifications as a control tactic
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempts to impose formal qualifications (e.g., college degree + experience requirements) on journalists can serve as a way to restrict press freedom and professional movement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a free trade provision requiring Canadian journalists to have a college degree and three years' experience to work in the U.S.; such measures are seen as threats to free expression (Peter Galliner's critique).

rubrics_metrics.name: State ownership and unwritten editorial norms
rubrics_metrics.description: In state-owned media systems, editorial decisions and news norms are shaped by ownership and political control; journalists may see themselves as civil servants and follow unwritten rules (e.g., 'We have to portray even negative things in a positive light').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pressure to make press financially self-supporting can encourage lightweight, sensational, and politically unthreatening content. Example: China—state ownership of outlets, strong editorial constraints, and the emergence of popular but politically safe news.

rubrics_metrics.name: First Amendment protections and historical context
rubrics_metrics.description: In the U.S., the First Amendment declares that Congress shall make no law abridging the freedom of speech or of the press; it was a reaction against English licensing/censorship and seditious libel laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This constitutional protection frames U.S. press freedoms but exists alongside other pressures (economic, advertiser, and political). Historical context explains why such protections were prioritized.
